hints: Think about what a voltmeter actually measures when it is connected between two different half-cells.
walkthrough:
Picture what $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ means**
Think of two separate half-cells joined together to make a complete cell. Each half-cell has its own tendency to gain or lose electrons. The voltmeter reads the difference between those two tendencies, that is the push that drives electrons round the external circuit.
Final answer: The potential difference / voltage between two half-cells / electrodes measured under standard conditions.

hints: Recall the two general features every cell diagram needs, a way to measure voltage and a way to complete the ionic circuit without mixing the solutions.
Think about which species are gases, ions in solution, or solids, and therefore when an inert Pt electrode is needed to carry electrons.
Decide how $Cl_2$ gas can be brought into contact with $Cl^-$ solution at a Pt surface, and what must be present in the iron half-cell.
walkthrough:
Build the complete circuit**
You need two separate beakers, one for each half-cell. Join the solutions with a salt bridge dipping into both solutions, and join the electrodes with wires through a high resistance voltmeter. That gives a path for ions inside and electrons outside.

Set up the $Cl_2 / Cl^-$ half-cell**
This half-cell has a gas and an ion, $Cl_2(g) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2Cl^-(aq)$, so neither can act as an electrode. Use an inert Pt electrode dipping into a solution of $Cl^-$, with $Cl_2$ gas bubbled over its surface through a delivery tube so gas, ion and Pt are all in contact.

Set up the $Fe^{3+} / Fe^{2+}$ half-cell**
This half-cell has two ions in the same solution, $Fe^{3+}(aq) + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}(aq)$, so again you need an inert conductor. Use a Pt electrode dipping into a beaker containing a mixture of $Fe^{2+}$ and $Fe^{3+}$ solutions. Label all species clearly.

Final answer: Two half-cells connected by salt bridge with wires to a voltmeter forming a complete circuit. $Cl_2$ gas bubbled over Pt electrode dipping in $Cl^-$ solution. Pt electrode dipping in solution containing both $Fe^{2+}$ and $Fe^{3+}$.

hints: Link electrical work to free energy using $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{cell}$ and find $n$ from the balanced cell equation.
Check units carefully, $F = 96500$ $\text{C mol}^{-1}$ gives $\Delta G$ in $\text{J mol}^{-1}$, so convert to $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Find $n$, the moles of electrons**
Look at the cell reaction: $Cl_2 + 2Fe^{2+} \rightarrow 2Fe^{3+} + 2Cl^-$. Each $Fe^{2+}$ loses one electron, so two $Fe^{2+}$ ions give $n = 2$ moles of electrons transferred. That is the $n$ in the formula.

Substitute and convert units**
Use $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{cell}$$ $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.59 = -113870 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$$ Divide by 1000 to get $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$: $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -114 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the cell reaction is feasible under standard conditions.

Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{cell} = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.59 = -113870$ $\text{J mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -114$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Identify oxidised ($Fe^{3+}$) and reduced ($Fe^{2+}$) species for this half-cell and their concentrations, remembering $z = 1$ for $Fe^{3+} + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Apply the Nernst equation to the iron half-cell**
For $Fe^{3+} + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}$, $z = 1$. Oxidised species is $Fe^{3+}$ at standard $1.0$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, reduced species is $Fe^{2+}$ at $0.15$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Lower $[Fe^{2+}]$ favours reduction, so $E$ rises above $E^{\ominus}$. $$E = 0.77 + (0.059/1)\log\frac{[Fe^{3+}]}{[Fe^{2+}]} = 0.77 + 0.059\log\frac{1.0}{0.15} = +0.82 \text{ V}$$

hints: Remember $E_{cell} = E_{positive} - E_{negative}$, here $Cl_2/Cl^-$ stays at standard value while the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ value has increased.
walkthrough:
Combine the half-cell potentials**
The $Cl_2/Cl^-$ half-cell is still standard at $+1.36$ V and acts as the positive cathode, while the iron half-cell is now $+0.82$ V. $$E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode} = 1.36 - 0.82 = +0.54 \text{ V}$$ This is the same as $0.59 + 0.77 - 0.82$. Because the iron electrode potential has increased, the overall driving force $E_{cell}$ is smaller than the standard $0.59$ V.
